strengths: The proposed methodology and the application domain are both interesting.
The idea of training a neural network and a symbolic regression model simultaneously, and aligning them in their respective optimization processes, is worthwhile and potentially novel.

It could be used in a number of applications where physical laws are known or, as is the case here, there are established equations that map the relationship that should be approximated by machine learning.
The interpretability of the end result, combined with the performance of a neural network training, motivates this approach.

It would be interesting to see the method applied to the discovery of known physical laws, like in the following work: Cranmer, Miles, et al. "Discovering symbolic models from deep learning with inductive biases." Advances in neural information processing systems 33 (2020): 17429-17442.
The application of memory modeling is also interesting; I am not aware of the application of PINNs to such psychological modeling problems.

Most of the knowledge-informed literature is on physics-informed, including in symbolic regression, but the methods can be applied to other domains where existing relationships have been expressed as equations, even if they are not physical laws.
There is a clear application to economics here, and expanding the perspectives to include similar applications could be helpful.
The idea of jointly optimizing an equation with a neural network is novel among symbolic regression (SR) algorithms to the best of my knowledge.
Figure 2 gives a clear overview of the algorithm.
The problem is interesting, as far as I can tell (I am not an expert in this area).
The method seems novel and the proposed interplay between deep learning and symbolic regression is interesting.
The model seems successful, judging from reported results.
The originality of the model lies in the novel combination of existing techniques (deep networks, denoising, and symbolic regression) and its application to the new domain (memory).

I would like to especially highlight the new alignment algorithms, proposed here to account for the CPU – GPU interaction in the model, and domain priors that, first, kept the symbolic regression equations within the realm of memory model equations, and, second, accounted for the noise specific to memory-related data.
The significance of this model is in providing the equations (e.g. in Table 2) that are concise and at the same time have a high explanatory power for the memory-related data.
Further analysis of such equations looks plausible and may be beneficial for the fields of psychology, cognitive science, and neuroscience.
The quality of this work is in the thorough empirical evaluation of the proposed model.

While the model itself is rooted in literature and thus alone holds the potential of being useful for the task at hand, the evaluation on a series of datasets and the ablation study shows that the model indeed leads to the improvement of the performance and that all model components are necessary for such an improvement.
weaknesses: The main weakness of this paper is in its presentation; the mix of methods and an application readers might not be familiar with requires clear explanations of deep learning, symbolic regression, and memory theory.

The mathematical notation is highly verbose, with subscripts for almost all variables, making loss equations (e.g., Equations 8 and 9) hard to parse and redundant; simplifying the notation would greatly increase clarity.
More explanation of the baseline methods would also help; DKT-F and FIFKT aren't fully explained, nor is the way that symbolic regression is integrated into their methods.
The one-sentence explanations in appendix B are not sufficiently referenced in the main text.
In the Background, a short explanation of at least DKT could replace a vague sentence that does not give much information to the reader and is rather subjective.
Greater clarity in the text on the background methods and the problem domain would really help.
Acronyms are rarely defined before use, and some acronyms are defined never to be used again (e.g., NODS).

The paper introduces terms such as "Genetic Symbolic Regression" (GSR) and "Denoised Neural Network" (DNN) without sufficient grounding in existing literature, making their precise meaning and novelty difficult to understand.

The use of "Temporal Neural Network" (TNN) to refer to all possible ANN architectures is problematic, as it conflates different types of neural networks with distinct mechanisms for handling temporal data.

It is unclear whether the main aim of the paper is to discover memory equations or to propose a new SR-based algorithm, and the paper does not explain why the joint optimization with a neural network is particularly effective for discovering memory equations versus other domains.
Missing comparisons to state-of-the-art SR algorithms that do not use joint optimization with a neural network should be included (e.g., expand Table 2).
Existing SR benchmark datasets such as SRBench and SRSD should be used to evaluate the proposed algorithm's equation discovery ability.
Missing error bars for empirical results make it impossible to tell if performance differences are significant (apart from Table 1 which performs a t-test).
Missing details on the selection of MLP architecture and tuning.
The choice of PySR as the SR algorithm is not justified; recent state-of-the-art SR algorithms (e.g., DSR [1], TPSR [2]) should be considered or reasons for exclusion provided.
I am mostly concerned about clarity, as the paper often uses confusing notation and undefined acronyms.
While the overall method is reasonably clear, it is not easy to understand the details or reported comparisons in performance.
The actual task is not fully described; Fig 1 mentions answers being "correct" or "incorrect", but the nature of the question for each word is unclear.
It is unclear what the final overall output of the model is (i.e., whether results are generated from the equation or from the neural network).
The notation is confusing and varies; a consistent notation such as 1:m for multiple timesteps and m for a single timestep is recommended.
Many undefined acronyms appear (e.g., KT in line 269, "KT-based framework").
The source of Beta_t in line 276 is unclear; the noise schedule equations resemble those used in diffusion models and should be cited.
Alternative methods in the ablation results are not described, making it difficult to understand what each alternative version represents.
It is unclear whether results are reported based on training a neural network alone (with or without denoising) and a symbolic regressor alone.
The "DKT" model is referenced multiple times in the baselines but never explained.
The text is often unnecessarily complicated despite the relatively straightforward idea of merging a deep learning model with an interpretable symbolic regression model and a denoising module.
Simplify Figure 2, remove the equations from it, or move it down the text to serve as a summary.
Simplify and reduce the length of equations (e.g., Equations 8 and 9) which occupy nearly half a page despite introducing simple concepts like mean square error loss.
Some results, such as the equations in Table 2, are present but could use further discussion.
The Methods section describing the model in sufficient detail to reproduce it (e.g., neural network parameters and training schedule) is missing.

The background section mostly repeats the introduction; consider shortening one of these sections and expanding the other with model details or using the vacated space for additional results discussion.
KT-based framework: KT is not defined in the main text.
MAE is not defined in the main text.
Table 1: second best models should be clarified as not including SPsyINN models.
Table 2 is not referenced in the results.
Table 3 should provide statistical significance test data, ideally with false discovery rate correction.
